Performance Artists Who Put Their Bodies on the Line
With its emphasis on embodied experience, performance provides a necessary counteraction to cheap political theater and the dissociation and isolation of our fractured, digitized society.

Why do a performance art festival tied to national political issues foregrounded in the midterm election? In a moment when cultural and political institutions are retreating from provocative stances into solipsism and leisure, and government funding for the arts is but one of the many areas being slashed by right-wing political operatives, it might seem like the opposite of common sense to be opening a museum dedicated to presenting and preserving the least marketable and most controversial aspect of contemporary art: performance.

Instead, the opening of the Performance Art Museum in Los Angeles, the first US museum dedicated to this ephemeral medium, has been met with tremendous support. This is because performance, with its emphasis on embodied experience, altered psychological states, challenging social dynamics, and the absurd, provides a necessary counteraction to the dissociation and isolation of our fractured and digitized society.

Since the early 20th century, artists have deployed performance as a medium for political commentary. Dada artists in Zurich and Berlin played with the emptiness of political speech in war-torn Europe while Mavo artists in Meiji Japan used cross-dressing and shock value to mock the nation’s entanglement in colonial wars in China and Russia. With the midterm elections unfolding against a backdrop of unrelenting genocide, the embodied stakes of performance serve to sharpen its critique. The influencer news cycle has shortened our attention spans from 24 hours, already a significant shift manifested via CNN and Headline News during the Gulf War and honed during 9/11, to a far shorter, dopamine-fueled spike of rage-and-crash out that can be repeated multiple times in a single day. The war on Gaza has both numbed us to atrocities in our feed, and disconnected us from our own bodies and communities as we quietly absorb the unspoken impacts of the violence that we outsource.

In the 1960s and 1970s, this absorbed violence erupted in the work of the Actionist artists including Hermann Nitsch , Rudolf Schwarzkogler, Valie Export , and Gina Pane. High Performance magazine was the first outlet to cover these artists in the United States and an emerging generation of artists informed by them, including Chris Burden and Kim Jones, who took significant physical risks in performances that openly critiqued the prolonged war in Vietnam. At the same time, the sexual revolution was underway and artists including Barbara T. Smith, Suzanne Lacy, and Johanna Went put their bodies on the line accordingly, looking at the pleasures and the risks of erotic life from feminist perspectives. Artist and poet Sue Dakin, the publisher of High Performance , ran a campaign for president as an independent candidate in 1984.

These histories inform the two-year Performance Art Museum initiative, High Performance: A 2 Year Conference for which my colleague Leon J. Hilton and I organized Public Spirits: A Performance Art Festival on October 23, 2026.

Emerging out of these practices and the magazine’s coverage of them, the 1980 Public Spirit festival, organized by the Highland Art Agents (including Paul McCarthy, Barbara T. Smith, Chip Chapman, John Duncan, and High Performance editor Linda Frye Burnham) through LACE, LA’s longest-running experimental art space, featured 60 artists and over 100 performances over two weeks in May and four weeks in October. Many of the works were staged in rooms at the American Hotel and were intimate in scale. Some, like the Feminist Art Workers’ Bill of Rights advocating for the ill-fated Equal Rights Amendment or The Waitresses’ Coffee Cauldron honoring women in service work, were explicitly political in nature. Many followed participant Allan Kaprow’s model for Happenings, being unscripted actions that turned absurd, comedic, or disturbing. Some involved singing, dancing, or traditional theatrical presentations — including a musical by Carole Caroompas about unreliable exes, a dance number by Nancy Buchanan about covert US intervention in Central America, and a play by Alexis Smith and Heidi Hardin titled “Stardust” that featured an unknown Whoopi Goldberg. The central, perplexing conundrum of the “nepo baby” arguably is this: Does the nepo baby possess talent, and is that talent to any degree independent of the considerable social and financial benefits bestowed upon said nepo baby from birth?

In I Regret I Am Able To Attend: A Life Among Artists (2026), photographer Jessica Craig-Martin, daughter of Irish painter Michael Craig-Martin and Jan Hashey (sometime artist but more successful real estate broker), chooses to quote Paul Auster, a giant of 20th-century American literature, in the introduction to her memoir: “Stories only happen to those who tell them.” The quote is meant to underline her insistence that this book is not a memoir, nor a narrative, only a collection of tales, thereby excusing any requirement for fact-checking or referencing, despite it very clearly being an exhaustive narrative of her life and that of her parents. The choice of quote also underlines the book’s tone: These stories are remarkable because of who they happened to, regardless of whether they are actually interesting or not. And that is how celebrity — the condition of being famous simply for being famous — works.

Craig-Martin weaves her parents’ experiences into her own, with several chapters throughout returning entirely to their lives as side quests, detailing which houses they bought and how they were decorated and who their friends were and how much money they earned, variously bouncing between London and New York and dragging the author between them. Where there is an excess of material and social detail, however — the name-dropping comes in lists — there is a mystifying sense of disengagement or interest in her parents’ own artistic enterprises. We are told what Michael did and what accolades he received but nothing substantial about Craig-Martin’s emotional or intellectual connection to his work. Her tonal detachment at attending, say, the first-ever performance of Gilbert George’s “ The Singing Sculpture ” (1969) cleaves a divide between her, dragged to the debut as par for the course of a daughter of a well-connected artist, and us, mortals who would have killed to witness this legendary moment in art history. What is present from the start is a keen eye for fashion, even if it is delivered via observations about how her mother was painfully more chic than the other parents picking their kids up from school.

The payment giant has had its first significant refresh since 2021, yet its famous wordmark hasn’t changed. So what’s new? And how far can a studio nudge a legendary brand that billions of…

The payment giant has had its first significant refresh since 2021, yet its famous wordmark hasn’t changed. So what’s new? And how far can a studio nudge a legendary brand that billions of people already know by heart? We find out.

It’s one of those logos you see pretty much every day but don’t think much about. Perhaps it’s because it means we’re about to spend some hard-earned cash. Or maybe we just don’t care. But you’ll know the Visa logo when it’s mentioned. It’ll flash up in your head as familiar as the faces of the people you love. So when you look at Base Design’s new identity for the brand, can you spot the difference?

That’s what I find most fascinating about a job like this. When a logo is so famous and features on a zillion cards and on shop doors all over the world, how much room does a design studio really have to play with? You certainly can’t rip it up and you can barely touch it. Yet Visa wanted to feel fresh for a new generation of spenders, so something had to give.

“When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn’t recognition. It’s relevance,” says Min Lew, managing partner and executive creative director at Base Design. “Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the net generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”

So what has changed? Three things, apparently. Base worked on the overhaul with Visa’s in-house studio to create a new symbol, a graphic device and a typeface. What’s interesting is that every one of them is borrowed from something Visa already owned.

The symbol, for example, is a ‘V’ lifted straight from the wordmark and it still has the little wingtip on its corner. This will begin to appear on some cards and across Visa’s digital assets, where four letters can prove to be a squeeze. Base stresses that it doesn’t replace the wordmark we all know and always appears alongside it. What it has ditched is the blue, white and yellow flag symbol that was introduced in 2021.

The typeface, Visa Sans, was created by Displaay Type Foundry and takes inspiration from the wordmark, too. It’s geometric for consistency at every scale, and its rounded forms hope to warm things up.

Then there’s the “hero graphic device”, a phrase coined by Base. It’s a bar, derived from the bands of the original Visa logo. Which sets us up nicely for a history lesson: when Bank of America launched BankAmericard in 1958, the name sat between a blue band and a gold one, and those bands stayed put when the card became Visa in 1976. They disappeared in the mid-2000s, leaving the wordmark to breathe on its own. Now those bands are back, sort of, as a single bar that can hold the wordmark, ‘V’ symbol or a message.

It’s only a tiny change but graphic designers will see it as the boldest. The wordmark can now be cropped at the bar’s right-hand edge, so ‘Visa’ runs off the side as if it’s pulling everything forward. It’s what Kellogg’s has done for ages, showing just a hint of the full wordmark and yet we all know exactly what it is.

“The most powerful identities are built on simple ideas with extraordinary depth,” adds Lew. “More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity. This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences. Each expression is distinct, yet unmistakably Visa.”
How far is far enough, though?

It’s worth taking notes from Visa’s last brand refresh. In 2021, Mucho redrew the wordmark, brightened the blue and then split the tricolour symbol off as an asset in its own right. Five years on and that symbol is being retired, yes, but Mucho’s wordmark has become the source material for everything else.
On asked how far it could go, Base seems to have said, backwards. It’s dipped into the archive and found something meaningful in the four letters themselves.

The Florida studio has created a full brand universe for Vollie, a new haircare company on a mission to “Bottle the salon”.

Salon-quality haircare at home sounds fantastic, doesn’t it? For precisely this reason, though, the number of competitors in this space is enormous. So if you’re launching a new brand, how do you convince people you’re worth investing in? That was the challenge facing Yungbld , an independent, female-owned branding and design studio based in Florida, when its founder was building a haircare startup called Vollie.
Yungbld set out to strike a perfect balance between premium and approachable. No mean feat, and they didn’t stop at a logo and a label.

“The founder came to us with an idea to ‘bottle the salon’ and a formula,” explains Laura Miller, founder and creative chief at Yungblud. “And we built the brand into a full visual universe spanning strategy, identity, packaging, product design, CGI and animation, launch imagery, and an immersive digital experience at vollieverse.com.”

The new brand evolved from a clever tagline: ‘Handle With Haircare’. It’s a neat play on the warning you’d typically see on fragile parcels, and beautifully sets up the tension the brand is built on. Namely, that haircare products are meant to be gentle by design, but powerful in performance.

“We developed the entire experience around the idea ‘Handle With Haircare’, using sleek forms, dreamy textures, soft shadows and a restrained palette to create something that feels both premium and emotionally warm,” says Laura.
That restraint shows most clearly in the colour system. Yungbld has limited the palette to three pastels—candy pink, lilac, and pale periwinkle—anchored by black and a cool grey.
In one of the launch images, the studio depicts this literally as a Pantone swatch strip held over a model’s face, listing 230 C, 2635 C, 2120 C, Black 7 C and Cool Gray 2 C.

To balance all that softness, the typography is based around heavy, chunky, all-caps sans-serif. Black and bold, it’s the perfect choice for the wordmark, a series of one-word campaign posters (Oiled, Glossed, Brushed, Stacked) and crossheads on the website.
On launch, Vollie’s range features three products: Super Soft, a softening and strengthening hair mask; Dream Defender, a prepare-and-protect hair oil; and So Glazed, a resurfacing gloss.
Each gets its own pastel. All three share a cylindrical bottle with a ribbed cap and a pointed nozzle. The wordmark is moulded into the bottle in relief rather than printed.
Yungbld also designed products beyond the bottles, including a wide-tooth comb with the wordmark running down its spine and clear tinted zip pouches that show the bottles inside.

The CGI work leans into that idea of ‘dreamy textures’, with generous use of pastel soft gradients. The live-action imagery, though, takes a different route: warm, grainy and purposely lo-fi; again, achieving a lovely visual balance.
Overall, this brand launch impressed me by its heady combination of confidence and scale.

It would have been tempting to launch Vollie with a brief Instagram teaser, and a nice bottle and not much else. Instead, Yungbld has come out guns blazing, crafting a full brand world where packaging, product, motion, photography, and web all benefit from a shared language.
It’s soft where it needs to be and bold where it counts… just like the haircare products themselves.

Su Blackwell Enchants with Folkloric Stories That Spring from Vintage Books
The artist's new exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us.

From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist Su Blackwell carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptures. Her latest body of work, opening this week in a solo show titled Pathway of Crumbs , draws on fairytales and folklore, a fitting topic for such dreamlike scenes.

Nodding to the enduring children’s story of Hansel and Gretel , the exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us. “In Flight,” for example, stretches nearly 3.5 feet as a swarm of butterflies emerges from the flared pages of a book. “Break off my Branches” is similarly dynamic, with a flock of multi-colored birds perched on the spindly stems that burst from a splayed edition.

Blackwell selected this particular set of books because they’ve been in her collection for several years, allowing the artist to digest their contents and ruminate on how they might emerge over time. Some she’s left in the same condition since purchasing them from a secondhand shop, and others she’s minimally cut and spliced for earlier projects. All, though, have remained a compelling artifact of human knowledge and a collective desire to create, one she transforms anew into striking compositions at the intersection of nature and culture.
Pathway of Crumbs is on view from November 25 to January 25 at Long & Ryle in London. Find more from Blackwell on her website .

British street artist Helen Bur completes her largest mural to date in Bordeaux's Grand Parc neighbourhood, celebrating motherhood, female solidarity and community connection through EXIT's…

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.

Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.

Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness . Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

A man flew from Manchester to Spain for a stag party using his wife’s passport by mistake, something that wasn’t flagged by staff at Manchester Airport.

Ben Moore told BBC Radio Stoke that the mix-up was only revealed when he touched down in Alicante and began queueing up for passport control. In the interview, he said, “I opened up the passport there and, to my horror, it was my wife’s photo on the passport.”
He then said, “I searched through all my luggage about eight times thinking there’s no way I could have got to Alicante without my own passport.”
Moore initially thought that he’d picked up both by mistake, used his own to get through customs back in Manchester before taking out the other one in Spain.

After all, Moore owns property in Spain and makes the trip multiple times a year. It was possible that he’d made a mistake while on autopilot. However, he realised that the only passport he had in his luggage belonged to his wife. Something that confused Spanish authorities just as much as him after he went to them and explained the situation. A process that Moore said the police officers there were “a little bit intimidating” about.

Moore’s trip ended early, with him being put straight back on a flight to the UK while his friends continued the stag party without him. The flight out from Manchester was operated by Ryanair, who have announced that they’ll be reviewing the matter.
However, they also stated that passenger document checks at the boarding gate are technically not carried out by the company themselves, but by their third-party ground handling provider Swissport.

BBC News reached out to Manchester Airport for comment, who said that the responsibility for checking passports lies with the airlines, as airports only ask for boarding cards from passengers when passing through security.

The day 10,000 women marched on Versailles and won the French Revolution
The original cost of living crisis.

If we think the current cost of living crisis is bad (and to be clear, it is), we should spare a thought for 1700s France , where a cost of living crisis got so apocalyptically bad it inspired the French Revolution.

While one can’t help but generalise when talking about a period of history as Earth-shaking as the French Revolution, it is true. One of the key things that turned the opinion of the French working class against the nobility was how expensive bread had gotten. Combined with the rumours that this was not due to a famine or a natural food shortage, but quite simply because Versailles was stockpiling it for themselves, and you’ve got a recipe for a serious regime change.

So, was this true? The history of the French Revolution is a messy one to wade through due to the sheer amount of propaganda on both sides racing around. Was Versailles really just hogging bread for themselves because they thought they had a God-given right to it? Not quite. Turns out that in 1788, destructive hailstorms combined with a brutal winter meant that the national stocks of grain ran low, causing the French government to pay through the nose for foreign imports.

This meant that the government had to place a high premium on grain and bread, which the working class of the nation couldn’t afford. The government tried to take the hit on this, capping bread prices at a more affordable cost and paying the nation’s bakers the subsidy to cover the difference. If we’re to believe the government reports of the time (who often had just as big a problem with Versailles as any of the working class), this nearly bankrupted the entire country.

Thus, the government tried one last roll of the dice. They completely deregulated the domestic grain trade, letting local merchants decide the prices for themselves, thinking class solidarity would mean they’d sell for an accessible price. Deregulating markets has literally never solved anything, though, and that was also the case here. The nation’s merchant class just held onto their grain stocks to increase its value. Considering this was based around food, who would be at the front lines of all this strife?
The class of people in France tasked with buying and preparing food for their families.

It’s true, the people at the forefront of this revolution were women, and on October 5th, 1789, they decided to do something about it. They were fuelled by the rage of not being able to buy more than scraps for their family while Versailles feasted on game and white wine; a riot started in a market in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine district of Paris. It consisted mainly of the city’s women who had been out to market that day and decided that enough was enough.

The riot grew and grew until there were enough people to storm Paris’ City Hall and help themselves to the local government’s food supplies. They didn’t find any there, but what they did find were weapons. This was the turning point for the whole revolution. Their plan (if you could call it that) was to burn down Paris City Hall, at least until the immortal words “À Versailles” were shouted by the known hero of the revolution, Stanislas-Marie Maillard.

This changed the whole makeup of the event. It suddenly went from a riot to a march. The assembled group, mainly made up of between six and ten thousand women, marched 12 miles from Paris to Versailles. How did they get there? Wasn’t there an army or a national guard of some kind to prevent them from leaving Paris? Well, there should have been. However, the mainly working-class members of the National Guard demanded to join the march. They were just as done with this shit as any other member of the working class.

Eventually, the mob arrived at Versailles. They refused to leave until a delegation was brought in to meet with King Louis XVI directly, where the king agreed to their terms. He finally signed the revolutionary decrees his nobility kept demanding he ignore, but it wasn’t enough. Too many people had starved over the past few years for King Louis to just do the bare minimum and be done with it. Especially when people were well aware that the weak-willed Louis could be just as easily bullied out of enforcing these reforms…

One Saliva Bubble: How David Lynch tried to go mainstream
"So, she said to him 'poo-poo on your pee-pee'!"

Considered by many to be the greatest piece of television ever made, Twin Peaks: The Return was a seismic moment even to die-hard fans of David Lynch because it proved one thing that no one saw coming.
His entire career before it had been him holding back.

Yes, baffling movies like Inland Empire , Eraserhead and Mulholland Drive had been Lynch not necessarily on easy mode, but definitely trying to curb some of his more esoteric traits and make his signature style more accessible to others. On the one hand, this is just as well. Twin Peaks: The Return left several people who weren’t high-minded TV critics baffled, confused and bored.

On the other hand, it does ask a tantalising question. What if Lynch tried to actively talk down to his audience and open himself up to making a full-on blockbuster? While his most accessible work, The Straight Story , is also his most low-key and low-stakes, it remains his biggest attempt at a blockbuster alongside Dune . His sole attempt at an adaptation, and one that still alienated several people for all the wrong reasons. What was Lynch’s idea of a film to get butts in seats?

Well, we actually have some idea thanks to his work in the aftermath of Dune . He was in dire straits after that film died a horrible death at the box office, and he was very lucky to get a gritty, somewhat grotesque crime thriller like Blue Velvet off the ground afterwards even at its tiny budget compared to the heights of Dune . Thus, after the success of that film steadied the ship, Lynch was paired with Hill Street Blues showrunner Mark Frost to begin work on the script of his next project.

After the duo initially began work on a shelved Marilyn Monroe biopic, they started work on their idea of a surefire hit, which became One Saliva Bubble . This is a script which really is levelled at the lowest common denominator at points. If you need an example, the inciting incident of the entire film involves a security guard at a military complex saying, “So, she said to him ‘poo-poo on your pee-pee!'”, and laughing so hard that he spits the titular bubble onto a console he’s guarding.

This causes a short circuit in a satellite it’s controlling, which then makes it shoot a laser beam onto a small town in Kansas, causing all of its inhabitants to swap bodies at random. This led to 90 minutes of slapstick fun built around a family man swapping bodies with a psychotic hitman, that Lynch himself described as “out-and-out wacko, dumb comedy”. To be clear, he wasn’t being entirely snooty about this, he said that he and Frost essentially spent the entire writing process thinking of things about the body swap premise that made them laugh and just crammed them into the script one after the other.
Considering they had just finished making Blue Velvet , I can imagine this was a refreshing change of pace.

What’s more, the script was a massive deal in Hollywood. Everyone who read it loved it and was willing to give Lynch a chance after a flop like Dune and a grim little thriller like Blue Velvet could have made him radioactive. Martin Short and Steve Martin signed up to star in the picture; all was set for work on One Saliva Bubble to begin. However, this was when Lynch still had a contract with Dino De Laurentiis’ production company, and six weeks before shooting was due to start, the company filed for bankruptcy.

What brings this full circle, though, is what Lynch and Frost did next. After two Hollywood projects in a row that stalled despite them not only working well together, but enjoying it too, their shared agent suggested they find a project that could work in Frost’s native medium of TV. Frost and Lynch went to a coffee shop in Los Angeles and started work on an idea that would combine the small-town absurdity and broad comedy of One Saliva Bubble with the crime thriller grit of Blue Velvet .
They came away with the pitch, premise and series outline for a little show called Twin Peaks . Not bad for a knucklehead comedy, right?
The Loneliest Orbit: Why Sci-Fi Needs the Gig Economy, Not Billionaire Fantasy
Daniel Zvereff, director of the new animated feature Moonfish , carefully considers the role science fiction should play in this current moment.

When I was a child, I’d lie in the yard at night, stare at the sky and dream about leaving Earth. My head was full of the rings of Saturn and the red dust of Mars, thinking about worlds where nobody had ever walked. The Apollo missions, the Soviet cosmonauts, the disasters and the triumphs: back then, it felt like proof that no matter how ugly geopolitics got down here, curiosity could still pull us forward together.

Maybe that was a child’s delusion, but our collective relationship with space has since changed into something almost unrecognizable. Over the past 20 years, space has become privatized. If you watch a commercial rocket launch today, the aesthetic is slick: carbon-fiber hulls, tablet consoles and bespoke spacesuits tailored to look good on social media feeds. Private capital sells off-planet travel like a venture-backed manifest destiny, an escape hatch for a ruined planet bought with tech fortunes. Billionaires pay for three minutes of zero gravity, holding up flowers in orbit for multi-camera livestreams cut like fashion commercials. Hollywood mostly plays along. Modern sci-fi gives us clean, digital environments where the actual misery of the void gets buried under good lighting and industrial chic. Characters fly pristine ships, solving crises through sheer heroic grit. It looks great on screen, but it ignores how human labor actually works on a frontier.

Every time people pushed into extreme environments to dig up resources, whether it was on Pacific whaling ships, North Sea oil platforms or in boomtown mines, the story was never about freedom. It was about exploitation: impossible quotas, broken bodies and deadening isolation. Right now, in the new digital frontier, data centers are chewing through power grids and overheating the planet to run algorithmic models. If a company ever sets up a permanent base out in orbit, they won’t be sending the upper class. Space is toxic, freezing and dangerous. The only people out there will be contract workers trapped inside heavy machinery, millions of miles from Earth.

When I started writing my animated feature Moonfish , I wanted to push back against the tech myth. Silicon Valley spent decades promising that a connected world would build an open, utopian paradise. Instead, we got algorithmic surveillance. Moonfish grew out of that frustration: an unglamorous, blue-collar survival story where the only thing keeping a person alive is the memory of home.

During the Cold War, filmmakers understood the importance of imbuing their vision with symbolism critical of their oppressors. In Tarkovsky’s Solaris , Stanislaw Lem’s station isn’t a monument to human genius; it’s a leaky, rusting psychological dump where instruments sit under layers of dust while the crew falls apart from grief. Filmmakers behind the Iron Curtain knew how to smuggle harsh truths through genre. They knew that technology doesn’t fix human nature; it just gives a faceless bureaucracy better ways to control you. Decades later, we live in the world they warned us about. Pretending a privatized orbital space station would run any differently is pure denial.

In Moonfish , the main character is just an off-planet contractor mining rock on an asteroid. He has a simple company rule hanging over his head: hit your extraction quota, or the transport ship leaves you behind. No quota, no pickup. His life is valued strictly by the weight of what he pulls out of the ground. The threat in the film isn’t an alien hiding in the dark, it’s a spreadsheet in a data center back on Earth, checking a box that says his life isn’t worth the fuel cost of bringing him back. Down here, we’re already living that way. Office workers have their keystrokes logged every minute. Gig workers get told that zero stability is just “flexibility and freedom.” A miner forgotten on an asteroid isn’t a sci-fi invention, he’s the direct continuation of a delivery rider pedaling through sleet, or a driver sleeping in a car to hit a surge bonus.

Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and bring back every little thing you did to look at ease. You remember where you put your hands and the joke you made while you worked up the nerve to ask them to stay. The relief came when they heard the question in the joke and stayed a little longer. It can take years to realize how much you miss being known that well.

At the opening of “Hush Now (The Calling),” Apolonia sings to a familiar face bathed in red light, as king them to drop the mask with the gentle insistence of an old friend inviting you to sit and stay awhile. The track is the lead single from Trip , the four-track EP released November 20 by Hamburg noise-pop trio Seasurfer .

Christian Klepp ’s footage casts the first verse’s red light across the stage. Red and yellow projections sweep the back wall, while green glints in the dark glasses above a ribbed microphone. Maysterwerke cuts from this intimate close-up to wider shots, where amber haze reduces the band to little more than silhouettes.
Watch the video for Hush Now (The Calling) below.

The way the band moves in and out of view has a counterpart in the arrangements Dirk Knight began imagining in New York. “For me, this is the sound of cities,” says the instrumentalist, who recorded, produced and mixed the EP. He keeps the bass and drums fairly still while the guitars and the voices of Apolonia and Kiora drift in and out of focus.

Those guitars have been a constant since Seasurfer’s first two albums on Saint Marie Records and through collaborations with Cocteau Twins’ Robin Guthrie and producer John Fryer. This year the band put them to work on the post-punk of June’s Angels , then let them fill the room on August’s shoegaze-heavy The Noise is ours . On their third EP of 2026, a trip-hop beat gives the guitar chords more room to ring.

You can hear that space in the first bars of the opening track , One . The guitars drone and the drums take their time, leaving room for the strings that Chandeen’s Harald Löwy adds to the arrangement. The higher voices blur into the chords the way they do on My Bloody Valentine’s Loveless . The low lead comes through with the intimacy of someone speaking in confidence. It’s a seductive way to sing about making peace with your own company and the knowledge that we come and go alone.
Watch the video for One, filmed by Ahmed Sarowar and edited by Dirk Knight, below:

That intimacy carries into Hush Now (The Calling) , where a sigh of synths stretches into long, luminous lines and Knight’s guitars bring warmth up from below. Apolonia and Kiora’s voices cascade through the chorus, opening the melody out the way Elizabeth Fraser could on Cocteau Twins’ Heaven or Las Vegas and Milk & Kisses . Apolonia describes the song as a memory of first love, and Kiora hears loss and longing in the words. When the refrain comes round to “I’m by your side,” the reassurance sounds as necessary to the person giving it as it does to the one hearing it.

The guitar comes further forward on “Disappear” , where the opening loop has the woozy repetition of Cocteau Twins’ Otherness EP. The voice has Cranes’ reserve and some of Portishead’s unease. When the drums drop away, the guitar keeps circling long enough for you to stop anticipating the next hit. By the time it comes, the loop has built up a charge that carries into the closing bars.

The drums make you wait for them again on “I See You” . The guitars pile up first, with the soft-edged distortion of Loveless , and the drum machine gives them a trip-hop lilt when it comes in. There’s some of Cranes’ distance in the singing and some of the poise of Siobhan de Maré on Mono’s “Life in Mono.” At under three minutes, the closer rewards a second pass. Follow a guitar you barely noticed the first time through, and you can hear the arrangement shift around it.

Last night marked the end of my birthday week, because spending last week in Paris wasn’t enough- I had to extend it. What a gig to wrap it up with! I’ve been waiting to see C.O.F.F.I.N for what has felt like a lifetime, and last night- I finally got to see them. What made it even more special was having Gold Cup as the support.

I’ve seen Gold Cup live this year about 4 times now, and they just keep getting better and better. Despite a few technical issues at the start, they played their set as if they were the headliners. And to be honest, it won’t be long until they are headlining the Pink Room at YES. Some bands are made to be heard live, and Gold Cup are one of those bands. There’s something about their live shows that just makes you feel good and glad to be alive, y’know? I can’t wait for their debut record to come out because it’s just going to make their shows even more wild. They’re the best at what they do, and it felt like the crowd were an even split of Gold Cup and C.O.F.F.I.N fans, and you cannot help but be proud of that. The energy they have on stage and the way they play together is a thing of beauty- and yes, you will leave feeling like you want to start a band because of them.

C.O.F.F.I.N time! Where on earth do I begin? Opening the set with Out In Oslo caused the room to erupt and it pretty much stayed like that for the whole time. Part of me was watching the band, the other part was just obsessed with the crowd. It is so easy to feel unsafe at shows especially when it’s rowdy, but this felt safe. It felt like a community. And as a visibly queer person, that feeling is rare to find right now given how shit the world is. But when you find that safety net, you hold onto it. I love everything that C.O.F.F.I.N stand for, and whilst the night was ridiculously fun- they used their platform to highlight the domestic violence rates in Australia, how corrupt governments are, calling people out on their shitty behaviours and not make life harder for those of us in marginalised communities. Life is tough enough already- just be kind to each other. It’s not hard.

Every song is yelled back at the band, and there are countless stage dives and crowd surfs. You could feel the love for the band in the room, truly. And the sense of being free and being able to express yourself however you want is also felt, and that’s something we should never take for granted. You can tell that the band not only love the bones of each other but they absolutely love playing shows, and you could feel how much it meant to them. I spent the time in awe of Ben because anyone who can sing AND drum at the same time is someone to admire (within reason because there are some people who can do it but y’know…)

Every song is greeted with people in the front throwing their sweaty bodies into each other and having the time of their lives. Some of them may be feeling it today but who cares! The joy on their faces, arms around their mates and strangers- it was so lovely to see because the world is unkind, but that energy did not step foot into the room once last night. What C.O.F.F.I.N have created with their music and live shows is a safe space, and that’s something to really hold onto. For me songs like Fast Love (this was my favourite and it was a tough call) and Give Me A Bite were WILD! Think Bad absolutely ripped too as did White Dog.

You really, really felt the love for the band when they left and everyone demanded an encore (and we got it!) They’re a band that you cannot help but love, and if you’ve not seen the documentary they recently put out- please go to YouTube and find it (it may still be there hopefully.) Not only will you too fall in love with the band and all they stand for, but you’ll just be in awe of their work ethic and how dedicated they are.

C.O.F.F.I.N are for everyone, and their live shows really make you feel it, and their live shows make you appreciate the band even more. I don’t know when they’ll be back in the UK but for now, I will hold onto this show as being one of the best things I’ve seen this year.

Thoughts of dread for the living.
Pandering with the queen of sorrow.

Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such a long negotiation with yourself that the place ends up closing long before you’ve picked up your keys. On “Feelings Are Monsters,” Berlin’s Night Nail give that dread seven eyes and seven legs. Brandon Robert counts them off as though taking inventory might make the damn thing easier to deal with.

Once upon a time, Robert was scraping by as a hired bassist in Hollywood, selling other people’s demos on the street, when a bandmate who put great stock in lucky numbers told him to “cheer up.” “It was degrading,” Robert says of those days. “But, we had to eat. Super dark times.”

“I decided that day to never play for someone else’s dream again,” Robert recalls. “I started recording my own music. I learned the hard way that no one tells your story for you. My bandmates actually did support me in my breakaway dream and ended up helping me tremendously with making my first singles and videos. But, I learned it’s really all on you to make it happen and rightfully so.”

That faith in lucky numbers has a sour afterlife in the refrain, where Robert sings, “Luck won’t change your number.” The track opens in a clatter, with bright flecks of guitar sticking out of the noise. Once the drums snap into time, the guitar winds through the sort of uneasy melody The Comsat Angels used to make sound inevitable, while the bassline lays down a gothic rock groove. A little over a minute in, Ruby Mai’s saxophone takes over from Robert’s low recitation. He comes back with his voice raised, then lets it sink in again, deeper, as he draws out his ode to the “queen of sorrow.” A rubbery bass break gives way to another round of counting before the guitar takes the song out.

Director Ilija Gavrilenko and editor Jean De Oliveira keep returning to the band under blue light, with black wisps spreading across the frame. Between those shots, a skull-faced figure in a wide black hat rides a lime-green scooter and lopes around a courtyard carpeted with fallen leaves. It looks like somebody sent a horror-movie ghoul out to run an errand.

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying…
Though they’d lost control of the outskirts of their town
and I loathe to tell you how it ends
so in silence we bow our heads

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying their miserable bills while history quietly buries the evidence. Human civilization has developed an extraordinary talent for committing atrocities, commemorating the dead, and finding fresh excuses to repeat the process. Somewhere in this grand procession of moral bankruptcy, Seattle’s Profit Prison has found sufficient inspiration to write a disco song about the unbearable weight of collective guilt.

The solo project of Parker Lautensleger, whose musical history includes Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel, and Excarnated Entity, has spent nearly a decade exploring the more psychologically disturbed possibilities of electronic pop. His latest single, In Memoriam, taken from the forthcoming album Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen? , sounds like Bronski Beat wandering into a particularly unpleasant historical reckoning, with electronic pioneer Gershon Kingsley conducting the proceedings from behind an enormous bank of synthesizers.

The arrangement possesses a strange, almost indecent sweetness. Synthesizers trace delicate melodic figures above a measured electronic rhythm, their crystalline repetitions creating the impression of a forgotten European dance record rescued from somebody’s flooded basement. Lautensleger sings with a trembling, distant resignation, his voice occupying the uncomfortable space between Neil Young’s wounded sincerity and the exquisite emotional distress of early synthpop by Das Kabinette, Depeche Mode, and others you might find on the Some Bizzare Compilation. Every syllable seems burdened by information its owner would dearly prefer to forget.

And what dreadful information it is. The lyrics describe a family whose apparently stable existence has been overturned by events unfolding near a border, where some unspecified act of violence has left questions that nobody seems willing to answer. Children inherit uncertainty, the dead receive their solemn acknowledgments, and the living are forced to contemplate the possibility that their own moral identities have been built upon carefully maintained ignorance. The song’s repeated interrogations grow increasingly desperate, suggesting a confrontation with somebody whose participation in an atrocity has become impossible to dismiss. Beneath the delicate electronic flourishes lies the hideous proposition that ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts of cruelty and subsequently spend entire lifetimes inventing explanations for themselves.

In Memoriam ‘s synthesizers maintain their patient, hypnotic progression while the words wander into the ugliest corners of human responsibility. You could conceivably dance to this record, which raises some rather uncomfortable questions about the emotional usefulness of disco. Lautensleger leaves those questions unanswered, however, allowing the music to continue its beautiful, merciless rotations while the accumulated weight of memory threatens to crush everything beneath it.

The video takes on a philosophical matter, as though we’re prisoners in Plato’s cave, watching distorted projections of events whose true nature remains somewhere beyond our comprehension. The road stretches onward, the lights assault our vision, and every image seems to conceal a fragment of some dreadful revelation.

The very British problem of GB Music Radio
GB News has launched an all-British radio station. As nationalistic thinkers so often do, they've oversimplified what it means to be British, and diluted the quality of their output in the…

How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.

What does access look like for disabled gig goers in 2026?
The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig

Attitude is Everything connects disabled people with music and live event industries, to improve access together. Starting in 2000, the charity has supported industry pros and organisations to help better understand and improve access for Deaf, disabled and neurodivergent people in music.

The charity’s State of Access Report - a report set up to set standards for national progress with disability in music - lays out exactly what that looks like in 2026, and how fraught with problems it can be, alongside the scale of the extra burden it places on disabled fans so they can safely enjoy their night out.
It’s the first report in eight years, and the first since Covid-19. In that time, the volume of the conversation around access in live music has hit a fever pitch.
It's partly out of necessity, given that Covid-19 has been described as a "mass disabling event", and as of 2023, 2 million people in the UK are estimated to be living with long Covid.

This fan-led review echoes similar calls to improve inclusion across music events. 24% of Music Fans Voice respondents disagreed (compared to 58% who agreed) with the statement that live music events currently reflect the demographic diversity of the UK.
There's a disability tax on attending live gigs

The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig, the most common of which (66%) relates to travel or accommodation. Other common access related costs include health or recovery costs (40%), personal assistant or companion costs (28%), higher ticket prices (25%) or food and drink for medical purposes (23%). Sadly, 58% of fans say extra costs have stopped them from attending an event.

The most frequent barrier disabled fans encounter relates to poor or inaccurate access information, which 69.5% of fans say they've experienced. Meanwhile, lack of seating or rest spaces is a barrier for 66.4% of respondents, booking or ticketing systems for 56.1% and staff attitudes or behaviour for 51.6%.
Access is inconsistent across the board

Only 20% of disabled gig goers say they feel they can consistently rely on their access needs being met. Even more starkly, 94% say they expose themselves to some level of risk when they go to a show.
The burden still falls on disabled people to advocate for themselves

72% of disabled gig goers have had to resolve access problems themselves, while 62% report having to explain their needs repeatedly. Just under half (48%) of respondents have said they've supported other disabled fans in the past, while more than half say they've had to leave events early due to access issues.
Fortunately, 58% of those surveyed said that they think access has improved in the last five years, and 61% would describe events as 'somewhat' or 'very' accessible.

"The findings from the survey are shocking, but sadly not surprising. But, by sharing the feedback with the sector, and supporting the music industry to embed access, we aim to improve the experiences for the disabled community, because by removing barriers, we don’t just open doors, we open up an entire industry."

This Junk-Drawer Staple Could Save Your Home in Case of Flooding, According to a New Study
A new study found that a surprisingly effective and cheap household tool blows sandbags out of the water when it comes to flood protection.

Flooding often brings to mind springtime thunderstorms and late-summer hurricanes, but this year, El Niño is serving up a nasty winter across much of the United States. Heavy rains and flooding are in the forecast for huge swaths of the country, leaving many wondering what they would do if water was bearing down.

Sandbags have been the go-to for centuries, but if you’ve ever tried to use them, you know they are a pain: heavy, labor-intensive and often not available when you need them. But now, researchers looking for inexpensive ways to help homeowners fight flooding have stumbled across something that blows sandbags out of the water.

Britain’s University of Hull released the surprising findings in a new report, and we have the results ahead. It turns out that something you no doubt have rattling around in your junk drawer or garage toolbox works better than sandbags—a lot better. Read on to learn an effective (and cheap) way to protect your home during a flood.
What junk-drawer staple can save your home from flooding?

That’s according to a new report called Testing the Performance of Low-cost, Temporary Property Flood Resilience (PFR) Solutions . The university teamed up with Flood Re, a partnership between the U.K. government and insurers, to pinpoint inexpensive ways for homeowners to protect their homes during a flood.

The results were amazing: Duct tape reduced water leakage 97% to 98% compared to a plain closed door. The much less common synthetic rubber tape (aka putty tape) did even better, with a 99% reduction. Even the worst-performing tape, yellow plastic tape, kept out 80% of simulated floodwaters during testing. And every single tape tested did better than sandbags, which reduced water intrusion by only 70%.

“Sandbags remain a symbol of flood protection , but these tests turn that assumption on its head,” said Jonathan Kassian, head of flood resilience at Flood Re. “What we have found is that some relatively simple and affordable products can do a much better job of keeping water out.”
Why does this work better than a sandbag?

For one thing, sandbags are porous, and they’re not designed to keep out water completely. Think of them more as a diversion tactic or obstruction, as opposed to tape, which can actually seal an opening through which water can flow.

In this study, researchers found that when placed in flood conditions of 0.2 meters (about 8 inches), sandbags leaked water at a mean rate of 584 liters per hour per meter, or 47 gallons per hour per foot. They were more effective in deeper water, but still only prevented, at most, 70% of water leakage . Sandbags are also heavy, time-intensive to deploy and difficult to place correctly.

Tape, on the other hand, is cheap and easy to store. It can be applied directly across gaps and conforms to irregular surfaces and openings where water can seep in. After the storm, cleanup is easy because tape is safely disposable, unlike sandbags, which absorb dangerous floodwater contaminants. And remember: Duct tape was more than 97% effective.
There is one caveat. Researchers concluded that how the tape was applied was “critical.” We’ll give you those details next.
How do you do this properly?

First, it’s important to understand that this was a research study about the effectiveness of certain barriers under testing conditions, not a how-to manual of using tape to stop a flood. But scientists were encouraged by the findings. Here are recommendations from the report:
Use a strong, wide tape. For duct tape, researchers recommend a width of 100 mm (roughly 4 inches).
Apply it to the flood-facing side. Tape performed best when it was applied on the outside of the door.

Cover vertical joints first. Tape the sides, making sure the vertical strip is attached to both the door and jamb and extends to the threshold. Then do the threshold and corners, overlapping the vertical strip.
Apply to clean, dry doors. To get the best adhesion, tape the door before wet weather arrives .
Make sure there are no openings. Avoid folds, press out any air bubbles and cover gaps.

That Sinking Feeling: A Race Against Time to Save a Pregnant Woman from a Car Submerged in Freezing Waters
A dazed pregnant woman drives into an ice-cold pond. Amid a sea of bystanders, one man takes action to save her life.

Shedly Apollon was awakened by a sound she couldn’t possibly sleep through: that of her car splashing into a pond … with her in it. Add in the rush of cold water pooling beneath her feet, and suddenly Apollon was fully alert, if disoriented. She was also fearing for her life. Actually, two lives. Apollon was in her 34th week of pregnancy on that cold morning this past February in Stuart, Florida, when she awoke to the reality that she was trapped in a sinking car .

Apollon, of nearby Port St. Lucie, had been on her way to a prenatal massage gifted by her fiancé, Woodly Sully. It was a birthday present. (Yes, this happened on Apollon’s 29th birthday.) Apollon had been struggling during her third trimester with preeclampsia, and as she drove to the massage, she began to feel woozy. She pulled her silver 2019 Hyundai Elantra over to the shoulder of Interstate 95, called Sully to let him know what was happening, drank some water, ate a little food and waited for the dizziness to subside.

After it did, about 10 minutes later, she got back on the road, but what happened next is a blur. Her car’s safety systems were beeping, telling her she was veering outside her lane, although in her haze-filled mind she was driving perfectly straight. She tried to pull over again, but started passing out. “I thought the car was in park,” Apollon recalls, “but in reality, it was still in drive.” And she drove off the right side of the road, straight into the pond.

When she came to seconds later to the sound of the splash, she unsnapped her seat belt and hit redial on her phone, then screamed to her confused fiancé, “I’m in a lake!” Within seconds, the call dropped. She and her unborn baby were all alone in a car that was listing, front driver’s side first, into a body of water.

Around this time, 29-year-old sport fisherman Logan Hayes of Sebastian, Florida, was driving down the same stretch of I-95 in his pickup, remarking to his friend and boss in the passenger seat, Chase Cornell, about how unusual it was that traffic was light and that they were running 20 minutes ahead of schedule on their work errand. “Something’s gonna happen,” Hayes joked.
Sure enough, Hayes soon saw brake lights ahead of him. And then the reason for the sudden slowdown: the Elantra, barely floating in the water.

Other cars had pulled over, but so far nobody had gotten out to help. So Hayes, also a professional surfer and confident swimmer, crossed from the far left lane across two other lanes, cutting off every car in his way, then pulled onto the shoulder and leaped out of the truck.
“Hey, is someone in that car?” he asked a bystander.

Hayes ran 50 yards down the highway, then a few more feet to the water’s edge, his eyes fixed on the Elantra. He was shedding clothing every step of the way. Off came his hat, his sunglasses, his shirt, his fishing boots, his sweatpants, his socks … until all he had on were his board shorts.

The outdoor temperature was in the mid-40s when Hayes hit the water around 8 a.m., and the pond was colder than that. But Hayes was surging with adrenaline and didn’t feel the chill as he dove in , trying to cover the distance as quickly as he could. He was underwater for a couple of seconds, then came up and took a few more strokes, and he was at the car.

With the vehicle tipping forward and to the left, the rear passenger door was the only one not submerged. Treading water, he pulled on the door handle, and it flew open. Scared and still struggling to get her bearings, Apollon was jolted by the sight of Hayes floating just outside her suddenly wide-open back door. “You have to get out of the car right now!” he yelled to her.
“You need to!” he urged. “You need to get to me.”

Apollon saw she’d have to crawl over the console between the seats—not easy to do in a car listing in the opposite direction, especially as her instinct was to move delicately and protect her belly. She swung her legs around so her feet were pointing toward Hayes. Now lying on her side, she pushed with her arms and slid up the console, inching toward the back seat, gravity working against her at every turn.

At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in Citizen Kane .”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for their own short adaptation of Poe’s story , which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films , you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer and B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman . Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton celebrated in animation at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe , a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on the playlist in various forms: an early D. W. Griffith feature , the directorial debut of Jules Dassin , an animated short narrated by James Mason , a British psychological thriller , and a transposition into modern-day New Orleans . And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Usher miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.

For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film Hidden Figures have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, in footnotes .

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “ Floating University ” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the Sorbonne , the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site Famous Scientists , “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the French Academy of Sciences . It would take another 51 years before the first woman, Marguerite Perey, a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more influential scientists and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a level of detail is unavailable in a museum, of course, but also difficult to access even if you owned the physical artwork in question. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured such luxuriantly digitized paintings as The Night Watch , Girl with a Pearl Earring , and The Garden of Earthly Delights . But there’s at least one celebrated work of Dutch masters whose viewing experience can never truly be replicated on the internet: the Ghent Altarpiece , also called the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb , by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.

After watching the video from The Gaze above, you’ll surely want to take as close as possible a look at the online Ghent Altarpiece , seeking out such highlighted details as the individual hairs on Adam’s beard, the realistically awkward expressions on the faces of the angel chorus, and the identifiable crucifixion scene pinned to a pilgrim’s hat.

But that may only stoke your desire to make a pilgrimage of your own, to Belgium, where you can see the real thing carefully placed in St. Bavo’s Cathedral. In the early fifteenth century, when that institution was called St. John the Baptist’s Church, its warden was the wealthy merchant Jodocus Vijd. Having endowed a new chapel, Vijd also commissioned the van Eyck brothers to create an altarpiece spectacular enough to secure him a spot in the afterlife. The result was one of the earliest masterpieces of oil painting.

Even apart from that designation (to say nothing of its being the most stolen work of art in history ), it has enjoyed an impressive afterlife of its own. Of the many who have traveled to behold it in situ at St. Bavo’s, some have no doubt sought the ecstasy of faith that can only be felt in a true holy place. But others have been thrilled, whether they were aware of it beforehand, by all the attention the artists put into integrating the work with its surroundings. The light within its images, for example, is painted in such a way as to match the light streaming into the cathedral itself. Those who look closely at the gem worn by the foremost singing angel will see a reflection of the very room meant for the altar. By the time their eyes meet the knowing gaze of the sacrificial lamb, they’re all but guaranteed to have a religious experience — though whether its nature is Christian, artistic, or otherwise will depend, as it does with all enduring art, on the individual viewer.

While the term ‘Friendsgiving’ is new, the tradition has been around for decades – found family and…
A food studies scholar provides some tips for throwing the perfect Friendsgiving gathering.

One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.

I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape.
While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.

My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.
If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.

As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering.

Modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era , when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved.

In her book “ Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality ,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event.

Within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity.

Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a new recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
